name: Battle of Barnet
date_note: Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471 (Julian calendar; 23 April by the modern calendar). Secure. Edward reached Barnet on the evening of 13 April and deployed in the dark; the Arrivall says the fight began between four and five in the morning and lasted about three hours, Warkworth from four until ten.
location_note: The point given is the road fork at Hadley Highstone, between the registered area (Hadley Green) and the Kitts End alternative. Treat it as the middle of a zone of possibility, not a site.
summary: Edward IV, back from exile, marched out of London on 13 April 1471 and in the dark drew up his army close to that of the Earl of Warwick, which was already in position north of Barnet across the road to St Albans. They fought at dawn on Easter Sunday in thick mist, with the lines misaligned so that each overlapped the other at one end. The king's left was broken and fled through the town, but in the confusion Warwick's army collapsed; Warwick and his brother Montagu were killed. Where exactly on this ridge it happened is not known.

name: Battle of Brentford
date_note: 1016; day and month not recorded. In the Chronicle it comes 'within two nights' of Edmund's relief of London, after Cnut's siege had begun in May and after Edmund's fights at Penselwood and Sherston, and before the battle of Assandun and Edmund's death on St Andrew's day (30 November). Summer is likely but is an inference.
summary: In 1016 Cnut's army besieged London. Edmund Ironside gathered a force, came to the city along the north side of the Thames and drove the besiegers to their ships. Within two nights he crossed the Thames at Brentford, fought the Danish army and put it to flight; many of the English were drowned, which the Chronicle blames on their own carelessness in going ahead of the army for plunder. Edmund then went to Wessex for more men and the Danes returned to London. That is all that is recorded. The scene shows the river, the ford and the banks as best they can be placed, with plain blocks of figures and shaded areas for where the armies may have been. Every one of those is a guess, and the model does not show the fight itself.

name: Boudica's sack of Londinium
date_note: AD 60 or 61; season unknown. Tacitus puts the revolt under the consuls Caesennius Paetus and Petronius Turpilianus (the consuls of AD 61), but many scholars prefer 60 on the grounds that the events need more than one year. The RCHME volume on Roman London prefers 60; MOLA writes 'AD 60/61'. A Bloomberg writing tablet dated 21 October AD 62 shows London trading again by then, which fits either year. Use 60 with a visible 'or 61'.
location_note: Site well known in general, not in detail. The pre-revolt town lay on the eastern hill (Cornhill) between the Walbrook and the area north of the bridgehead, with some occupation west of the Walbrook and a suburb at the south end of the bridge in Southwark. The burnt horizon has been recorded on many City sites (King William Street, Lombard Street, Eastcheap, Miles Lane, Fenchurch Street, the Walbrook west bank) and beside the road at the Southwark bridgehead. The point given is an approximate centre of the early town, not a find spot.
summary: During the revolt led by Boudica of the Iceni, the governor Suetonius Paulinus reached Londinium ahead of the rebels, judged he had too few troops to hold it, and withdrew, taking those who could march with him. The rebels then destroyed the town and killed those who stayed. Excavation across the City and at the Southwark bridgehead has found a layer of burnt debris of this date. The town was rebuilt within a few years and a fort was built on the eastern hill about AD 63.

name: Battle of London Bridge
date_note: Uncertain. Snorri places it after Swein Forkbeard's death (February 1014) as part of Aethelred's return, hence the usual '1014'; Hagland and Watson accept 1014 following Ian Howard's chronology. Olaf's early career is poorly dated and he is also associated with Thorkell's army, which attacked London unsuccessfully in 1009-10, so some place his London fighting then, and on the Danish side. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 1014 says only that Aethelred came home in Lent and was gladly received.
location_note: The place is known; the event is not. A timber bridge existed by about 1000 (first phase built of timber felled c. 987-1032) on roughly the line of the later medieval bridge, a little downstream of the present London Bridge, with Southwark at its south end. The point given is approximate mid-river on that line.
summary: Aethelred returned from exile in 1014 after Swein's death and recovered his kingdom; London was central to that. Norse court poetry composed for Olaf Haraldsson credits him with fighting at London and, in one stanza, with breaking 'Lundúna bryggjur'. About two centuries later Snorri Sturluson built these verses into a detailed story of Olaf's ships pulling the bridge down. No English source mentions such an attack. The bridge here is not shown falling.

name: Battle of Brentford
date_note: Summer 1016; day and month not recorded. In the Chronicle's sequence it follows Cnut's siege of London (begun about May), Edmund's fights at Penselwood and Sherston (after midsummer) and his relief of London, with Brentford 'two days' after the relief. It precedes Assandun (18 October 1016).
off_map: About 15 km west of the modelled area, up the Thames.
location_note: Poorly known. The Chronicle says only that Edmund crossed the Thames at Brentford. The Victoria County History notes the place-name is usually taken to mean the ford over the Brent, though a Thames crossing is possible, and that stakes on the foreshore at 'Old England' (near the Brent-Thames confluence, by Syon) may have defended a ford; it places the 1016 fight on the south bank. The point given is the approximate Brent-Thames confluence and is a placeholder, not a located battlefield. No archaeology of the battle is known.
summary: In 1016 Cnut's army besieged London, digging a ditch on the south side and dragging its ships to the west of the bridge. Edmund Ironside relieved the city, and two days later crossed the Thames at Brentford and fought the Danish army, putting it to flight. Many of the English were lost by drowning, which the Chronicle blames on their own carelessness in going ahead of the army for plunder. Edmund then went to Wessex to raise more men and the Danes returned to besiege London.

name: Battle of Barnet
date_note: Easter Sunday, 14 April 1471 (Julian calendar). Secure. Edward left London about 4 pm on 13 April and deployed in the dark; fighting began around dawn. Warkworth says about 4 am to 10 am; other accounts imply a shorter fight.
off_map: About 17 km north-north-west of the modelled area, on the Great North Road.
location_note: The general area is certain (north of High Barnet along the old St Albans road); the exact battlefield is not. English Heritage registered a battlefield in 1995 centred on Hadley Green / Monken Hadley, following a National Army Museum report. The 2015-18 Barnet Battlefield Project (University of Huddersfield, with the Battlefields Trust and Barnet Museum) concluded 'we cannot accurately identify the battlefield': sources agree it lay between half a mile and a mile north of the town, the terrain of the former Kicks End (Kitts End) Common about 1.9 km north of the Barnet boundary best fits them, and Hadley Green is 'problematic'; but metal-detecting found no conclusive battle scatter. Watson (2022) gives the current best guess as a circle of 1 km radius centred on Kitts End. The point given is near Hadley Highstone, between the registered area and Kitts End; treat it as the middle of a zone roughly 2 km long, not a site.
summary: Edward IV, returned from exile, marched out of London on 13 April 1471 and deployed at night close to the army of the Earl of Warwick north of Barnet. The armies fought at dawn on Easter Sunday in thick mist, their lines misaligned so that each overlapped the other at one end. Edward won; Warwick and his brother John Neville, Marquess Montagu, were killed. Their bodies were displayed at St Paul's, and Edward went on to defeat Margaret of Anjou's army at Tewkesbury on 4 May.

name: Midsummer sunrise along the axis, c. 2500 BCE
date_note: Late June (about 21 June by the solar year) in the sarsen-circle era. The year is a representative one inside 2580 to 2400 BCE; the day is the solstice by astronomy, not a recorded date.
summary: Looking from inside the circle north-east along the monument's axis, past the Heel Stone and down the first stretch of the Avenue, towards where the sun comes up on the longest day. The scene's one fixed sun is NOT moved: the white line and sun disc are an overlay marking the computed direction (azimuth about 48 to 49 degrees), not real lighting. For 2500 BCE, with the sun's upper edge just visible and standard refraction, the sunrise point is at azimuth 48.2 degrees on a flat horizon or 49.2 degrees if the horizon is raised 0.6 degrees. The Avenue's first straight stretch leaves the stones at about 49.9 degrees (from OpenStreetMap mapping), and the Heel Stone lies at about 51 degrees from the centre, so the sun rose slightly to the left of both. The true horizon height to the north-east was not taken from any source read.

name: Midwinter sunset through the Great Trilithon, c. 2500 BCE
date_note: Late December (about 21 December by the solar year) in the sarsen-circle era; a representative year inside 2580 to 2400 BCE, the day fixed by astronomy.
summary: From the Avenue, 110 m north-east of the centre, looking south-west through the circle at the Great Trilithon on the day of the shortest sun. As in the sunrise episode the scene's single fixed sun is not moved: the line and disc are an overlay marking the computed sunset direction. For 2500 BCE, upper edge just visible with standard refraction, the sun set at azimuth 231.0 degrees on a flat horizon or 230.0 degrees if the horizon is raised 0.6 degrees, within about a degree of the reverse of the Avenue's first stretch (229.9 degrees). Ruggles favours midwinter as the more important of the two solstices, and Parker Pearson cites the midwinter feasting at Durrington Walls; that is interpretation. The horizon height to the south-west was not measured from any source read.

name: Raising the sarsens
date_note: c. 2560 to 2470 BCE in the model; the sarsen circle is dated 2580 to 2475 BCE and the trilithons 2585 to 2400 BCE (93%) by the English Heritage Bayesian model. The day is arbitrary.
summary: The great sarsen stones go up. The sarsen circle (30 uprights carrying a ring of 30 lintels) and the five trilithons are built over perhaps a century; the model shows the circle part-way through. The stones were dragged from the Marlborough Downs, about 25 km north, and shaped on site; the lintels were fitted with mortise-and-tenon and tongue-and-groove joints borrowed from carpentry. How they were moved and raised is not known: the stones rising smoothly from the ground is the site's way of showing 'under construction', not a method.

name: Midwinter feasting at Durrington Walls, c. 2500 BCE
date_note: Late December in a representative year of the village's decade or so of use (c. 2515 to 2480 BCE in the model). The village is dated 2600 to 2500 BCE (2007 release) and, by later modelling, to roughly 10 to 12 years ending 2500 to 2460 BCE.
summary: A village of small square houses with clay floors stands inside the great timber ring at Durrington Walls, about 2.8 km east of Stonehenge on the Avon. Pig teeth from the site point to animals slaughtered in the winter, and the Southern Circle there is oriented to the midwinter sunrise; the usual reading is that people came here for midwinter feasts and, after the village was abandoned, the timber ring was replaced by a henge bank. How many houses there were and how many people came is not known, and none are drawn.

name: Bush Barrow burial, c. 1900 BCE
date_note: Wikipedia gives c. 1950 BCE for the burial and the Wilsford G7 group 2000 to 1800 BCE; 1900 BCE is a display year inside the uncertainty.
summary: Bush Barrow, on the Normanton Down ridge about 1.1 km south-south-west of Stonehenge, is a large round barrow about 49 m across and 3.3 m high, holds a rich Early Bronze Age burial with gold, dated about 1950 BCE. The gold lozenge plate measures about 184 by 156 mm. Round barrows of this period fill the ridges around the stones; here the scene is the barrow standing new on the skyline. Who was buried there is not known from the research notes.

name: Amesbury Abbey founded, 979
date_note: c. 979. The foundation date is approximate; the day is arbitrary.
summary: A Benedictine abbey is founded at Amesbury, in the Avon valley east of Stonehenge, by Queen Aelfthryth. It later becomes a Fontevraud priory (1177) and is dissolved about 1540. What it looked like in 979 and where exactly it stood within Amesbury are not known from the sources read; the precinct on the map is a conjectural rectangle by the church, and the buildings are placeholders.

name: Inigo Jones surveys Stonehenge for James I, 1620
date_note: 1620; the fraction 0.6 is an arbitrary display value, no month is known from the sources read. The survey and the Duke of Buckingham's digging are both given as 1620, though English Heritage also says 'the 1620s'.
summary: King James I, visiting Wilton House in 1620, asks the architect Inigo Jones to survey the stones. Jones's plan (published by his pupil John Webb in 1655) shows an idealised, regular monument which he reads as a Roman temple. The same year the Duke of Buckingham has the centre dug, the first known excavation there. The view shows the stones as they are thought to have stood, with the great trilithon down and the south-west trilithon still standing; which stones stood or lay in 1625 is largely inferred. Jones's plan is a restoration, not a record.

name: Robin Hood's Ball causewayed enclosure, c. 3550 BCE
date_note: 'Centuries around 3500 BC' (English Heritage); Wikipedia: probably built c. 4000 BC, possibly used to c. 3000 BC. Low confidence.
off_map: Robin Hood's Ball lies about 3.8 km north and 2 km west of the stones, 1 km beyond the north edge of this map, so it cannot be shown here. It is an earlier Neolithic causewayed enclosure with two ditch circuits and low banks, never comprehensively excavated.
summary: One of the first lasting monuments of the Stonehenge landscape, a causewayed enclosure on high ground north of the later Cursus, built when the ditches were fresh white chalk. Its size, internal features and end date are not known.
